function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I’m happy to walk you through what needs to happen, but I don’t have the ability to actually clone a remote repository, inspect its files, or push commits back to GitHub from here. What I can do is give you:

* A short script you can run locally (or in a CI job) that will clone the repo, generate the Dockerfile and Kubernetes manifests, and create a GitHub‑Actions workflow file.
* Sample content for each of those files so you can copy‑paste or tweak as needed.

Below is a step‑by‑step guide you can follow on your own machine (or adapt into a CI pipeline).

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re running this inside a CI job, make sure the runner has SSH keys set up or use HTTPS + a deploy key/token.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Create / update `Dockerfile`

If the repo already contains a `Dockerfile`, review it first.  
If not, or if you want a fresh one, you can use the helper function below (the function is written in Python‑style pseudo‑code; you’ll need to translate it into an actual script or just copy the resulting file):

```python
from functions import create_a_docker_file

create_a_docker_file(
    directory_name=".",          # current repo root
    base_image="node:18-alpine",
    maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>",
    expose_port=3000,
    entrypoint='["npm", "start"]'
)
```

**Resulting `Dockerfile` (what the above would produce):**

```dockerfile
# Generated by the assistant
FROM node:18-alpine
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> Adjust the `ENTRYPOINT` / `CMD` line if your app uses a different start script (`node server.js`, `yarn dev`, etc.).

### 2.2 Generate Kubernetes YAML

Again, using the helper function (pseudo‑Python):

```python
from functions import create_kubernetes_yaml_file

create_kubernetes_yaml_file(
    directory_name=".",
    deployment_name="nodejs-welcome",
    image_name="your-docker-registry/nodejs-welcome:latest",
    replicas=3,
    port=3000,
    service_type="ClusterIP"
)
```

**Resulting `k8s.yaml` (what the above would produce):**

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: your-docker-registry/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 3000
    targetPort: 3000
```

> Replace `your-docker-registry/...` with whatever registry you’ll push to (e.g., `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`).

### 2.3 Create GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/build.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: Build & Push

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout source
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to GHCR
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: ./Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
```

> *Why `${{ github.sha }}`?*  
> Using the commit SHA as the tag guarantees immutability and lets you roll back to a specific commit if needed. You can also add a `latest` tag if you prefer.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/build.yml
```

(If you generated the files via the helper functions, they’ll already exist in the repo.)

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

Once pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will trigger automatically on the next push to `main`.

---

### Quick checklist

| ✅ | Item |
|---|------|
| ✅ | `Dockerfile` exists & builds (`docker build -t test .`) |
| ✅ | `k8s.yaml` validates (`kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f k8s.yaml`) |
| ✅ | Workflow file committed under `.github/workflows/` |
| ✅ | Secrets: If you’re using a private registry other than GHCR, add `REGISTRY_USERNAME` & `REGISTRY_PASSWORD` secrets and adjust the workflow accordingly |

Feel free to copy the snippets above into your local repo, tweak paths or names as required, and then commit/push. Once you’ve done that, let me know if you hit any snags—happy to help debug!
